_comment: Shape of the M1 movement playground. This is a TEST AREA, not the Meadows. Its only job is to give walking, sprinting, jumping, camera orbit, stamina and fall damage something honest to work against; a flat field proves none of them. The real Meadows is authored later against docs/reference/tetherbound-meadows-keyart.png and replaces this wholesale.
_authored_not_procedural: Per the owner's direction, terrain is authored macro geography. The noise here is a deterministic recipe for one specific test area, seeded and fixed, not a world generator. Nothing at runtime generates terrain; this is baked to disk once and loaded as data.
_comment_world: Playground edge in metres. A few minutes of walking end to end: large enough that the horizon is not always in view, small enough that it stays a playground rather than a map.
_comment_region: Terrain3D's storage granularity, NOT the world size. world_size must be an exact multiple of it, or the baked image straddles region boundaries and leaves flat unfilled gaps inside partially-written regions. 512 over 256 fills exactly four regions.

hills._comment: The base rolling ground. Low frequency, gentle. This is what most of the walking happens on.

detail._comment: Surface break-up so slopes are not billiard-smooth. Small enough not to trip the character controller's step offset.

valley._comment: One broad low basin, so there is somewhere that reads as down. Centre is in world metres from the region origin; radius is where the depression fades out entirely.

rises._comment: Steeper rocky ground, for testing slope limits and fall damage. `sharpness` above 1 makes the sides steeper than a cosine bell; these are the only places the 45-degree slope limit should actually bite.

spawn_pad._comment: A gently flattened area around the player's start, so the first thing anyone tests is not a slope. Blends back to natural ground by `radius`.

_comment_colour: Slope-driven ground colour, written to Terrain3D's colour map. It MULTIPLIES the PBR albedo — it does not replace it. These were authored when the colour map was the entire ground treatment and there were no textures at all; they stayed after the textures arrived, and grass albedo at luminance 0.40 times a #496c34 map at 0.36 is a surface of 0.14 before any light reaches it. That is the whole reason the near field measured 0.096 against 0.27-0.60 across the references, and why no amount of sun, shadow, ambient or normal tuning moved it: nothing was wrong with the lighting.
_comment_colour_now: Near-white, so this modulates rather than paints. The textures carry the colour; this carries the slope-driven variation and the macro break-up that stops a 2K tile reading as wallpaper. Keep everything here above roughly #c0 — below that it is a brightness change wearing a colour's clothes, which is the mistake this comment exists to stop being repeated.
_comment_shader: Terrain3D shader settings. Every one of these is TUNABLE presentation and none of them touches collision or height — the bake is authored data and this is only how it is drawn.

shader._comment_background: 2 = NOISE. It was 1 = FLAT, which draws an infinite plane at y=0 past the baked 512m and fogs it to a uniform sheet. That produced a measured 0.146 luminance step across the ENTIRE width of `03-rise-overlook` at row 252 — the blind critic found it independently and called it the first thing the eye lands on. Noise gives the distance real shape instead, so the world stops having a visible edge.
shader._comment_blend: How far into the baked regions the noise blends. Too low and the seam comes back as a ring instead of a line.
shader._comment_macro: Macro variation tints the ground at two large scales, which is the only thing that stops a 2K tile reading as tiling. The critic measured the previous ground as high-frequency mottled noise with 'no blade direction and no scale cue' — a texture repeating every few metres with nothing varying above that.
shader._comment_macro_multiply: These MULTIPLY the albedo — the shader does `macrov = mix(colour1, white, noise1); macrov *= mix(colour2, white, noise2)`. So they can only ever darken, and two mid-tones compound: the first attempt used #c6d18a and #8fa06a, which multiply out to roughly 0.47 at their overlap and took the near-field ground from luminance 0.124 to 0.054 — a black foreground in every frame. Keep both near white and let them tint, not shade. Anything below about #b0 here is a brightness change wearing a colour's clothes.
shader._comment_dual_scale_removed: Terrain3D's dual-scaling uniforms (dual_scale_texture/near/far/reduction) are NOT reachable through set_shader_param on this build — the shader only compiles them in behind a feature this API does not expose, and writing them returns quietly having done nothing. They were configured here for two rounds while the surveys came back byte-identical. `_apply_ground_shader` now reads every uniform back and warns by name, which is how this was finally caught.
shader._comment_auto: Auto shader thresholds: how readily slope switches from grass to the overlay texture.

_comment_textures: Real PBR ground, replacing the `show_colormap` debug view that stood in for it from M1 to the first art pass. Terrain3D's auto shader picks texture 0 on walkable ground and texture 1 on slopes, so the grass/soil/rock intent the bake already encodes is expressed with albedo and normal detail instead of flat vertex colour. `uv_scale` is metres per tile: too large and the ground is mush at distance, too small and it visibly repeats.
_comment_uv_scale: Metres per tile is 1/uv_scale, so 0.34 tiles every ~3m. It was 0.18 (~5.5m), and at that size the near ground showed the photograph's own brown patches rather than its average — a green meadow with a brown foreground, reading as two materials. Tighter tiling averages to grass; too tight and it visibly repeats, which is what the macro variation and detiling above are for.
_comment_normal_depth: The most consequential number in this file. A photographic grass normal map at full strength turns most of its texels away from a 52-degree sun, and the ground within ~30m of the camera goes black — measured at luminance 0.071 against 0.27-0.60 across the references, with exactly the high-frequency mottled fizz the critic described. It flattens with distance because the mip average cancels the perturbation, which is why the far hills looked correct and the foreground did not. Raise it for more relief; if the near ground starts crushing to black again, this is the cause.
_comment_detiling: Rotates and shifts the tile per region so a 2K texture stops announcing its own repeat period. Together with the shader's macro variation, this is what separates 'ground material' from 'wallpaper'.

textures._comment_which_grass: Grass008, chosen by tools/rank_ground_textures.py rather than by eye — which is how the previous two were chosen and how both went wrong. Scored on the defect the critic actually named: long thin dark filaments, the 'cracked plates' signature. Grass008 measures 0.64 against Grass005's 4.37 — nearly seven times fewer — at the same luminance and saturation, so nothing downstream needed retuning.
textures.name: grass
textures._comment_normal_depth: Cut from 0.30 to 0.12. Flat, BOTH textures look like grass — the 'fractured plates with dark fissure lines' the critic measured were RELIEF, not albedo: a photographic normal map at a grazing view angle carves shadow valleys that read as cracks in stone, and mip averaging smears them into plates at distance. This is the knob for that, not the texture.
textures._comment_tint_round4: Lifted from #b9cf82. The tint MULTIPLIES the photographic albedo, so it is the knob that decides how dark the ground can be before any light reaches it. Raised toward white and pulled toward neutral: a multiply cannot desaturate, but lifting value turns the critic's 'maximally saturated near-black olive' into olive, which is most of the complaint.
textures._comment_uv_round4: Halved the tile from ~1.8m to ~0.9m. Lifting the albedo moved near-field luminance 0.28 to 0.33 exactly as the multiply model predicted, and the ground STILL read as cracked rock — because the darkness and the cracks are different problems. The cracks are the photograph's own dark gaps between grass blades, and at a 1.8m tile they are metre-scale features that the eye files as fissures in stone. At 0.9m the same gaps are fine texture. This is the knob for that; `normal_depth` was the knob for the RELIEF version of the same complaint and is already down at 0.12.

textures.name: rock
textures._comment_uv_scale: Metres per tile is 1/uv_scale, so 0.34 tiles every ~3m. It was 0.18 (~5.5m), and at that size the near ground showed the photograph's own brown patches rather than its average — a green meadow with a brown foreground, reading as two materials. Tighter tiling averages to grass; too tight and it visibly repeats, which is what the macro variation and detiling above are for.
textures._comment_normal_depth: Rock keeps more relief than grass. A cliff face with no normal detail reads as painted, and it is not the surface the player stands on at close range.

_comment_colour_round4: Lifted with the texture tint, because the two MULTIPLY and neither alone has the headroom. The photographic albedo's own value is 0.52; times the old tint (0.81) times the old colour map (0.83) is 0.35 before a single light touches it, and frame_stats measured the result at 0.12-0.43 near-field luminance against Palworld's 0.28-0.60. This map is BAKED — changing it means re-running build_playground_terrain.gd, which is why it is easy to forget it is part of the answer.
